articles.title: Securing equipment emerges as new variable for Korea's chip expansion plans - The Korea Times
articles.summary: Securing equipment emerges as new variable for Korea's chip expansion plans  The Korea Times
articles.full_text:
ASML not accepting orders for 2029, 2030
Securing equipment for manufacturing advanced memory chips is emerging as a new variable in Korea's plans to expand semiconductor production capacity through large-scale industrial clusters, after ASML, the dominant supplier of advanced chipmaking equipment, warned that its current production plans may not be sufficient to meet demand in 2027 and 2028.
During its earnings call Wednesday, ASML CEO Christophe Fouquet said the company's plans to increase its production capacity for advanced chipmaking equipment by 30 percent in 2027 and another 30 percent in 2028 would likely not be enough to meet customer demand.
“Last quarter, we talked about 30 percent more capacity next year, and also the aspiration to have another 30 percent increase in 2028,” Fouquet said. “But to be honest, it's becoming very clear that 30 percent in 2027, 30 percent in 2028 will not allow us to meet our customer demand.”
According to the company, the planned capacity increases cover both low-numerical-aperture extreme ultraviolet (low-NA EUV) lithography equipment and deep ultraviolet (DUV) immersion systems.
EUV equipment is used to produce extremely fine circuit patterns for advanced semiconductor chips, while DUV immersion systems are used for a broader range of patterning processes. Both are critical to manufacturing high-performance memory chips produced by companies such as Samsung Electronics and SK hynix.
“So a lot of our discussions with our customers now are shifting in fact beyond 2027,” Fouquet said. “A lot of order intake for 2028. But also some strong interest to already place orders for 2029 and sometimes even 2030."
The supply bottleneck anticipated by ASML could become a major variable in Korea's ongoing plans to build large-scale semiconductor industrial complexes in Yongin, Gyeonggi Province, and Jeonnam-Gwangju Special Metropolitan City.
In Yongin, two separate semiconductor clusters are planned, each housing fabrication facilities of SK hynix and Samsung Electronics. SK hynix has already begun construction of its fabrication facilities, while Samsung is scheduled to break ground later this month. Separately, the two companies plan to build large-scale semiconductor manufacturing sites in Jeonnam-Gwangju, upon the government’s push.
The two companies declined to confirm the status of their equipment orders, but industry officials said a supply bottleneck could materialize if strong demand persists beyond 2030.
“It is difficult to describe the current situation as a bottleneck. Given that ASML is expanding its production capacity, it is hard to expect that orders placed now would face delays significant enough to call it a bottleneck,” an industry official said. “However, if the current strong demand persists over the long term, supply bottlenecks could emerge.”
In the semiconductor industry, the lead time for equipment orders — the period between placing an order and receiving the equipment — typically ranges from 18 months to two years. This suggests that the current supply situation largely reflects orders placed around 2025.
The concern is that supply bottlenecks could materialize if demand remains strong or continues to grow through 2028, 2029 and 2030, coinciding with Korea's planned fab expansions.
In Yongin, SK hynix is targeting October next year for the start of production at its first fab, with equipment deliveries expected to accelerate as construction of additional fabs pick up speed. Samsung Electronics is also planning to begin operations at its first Yongin fab in 2029.
The outlook is more uncertain for the cluster in Jeonnam-Gwangju Special Metropolitan City.
Although neither company has officially announced a construction or operation schedule for their planned fabs in the region, local authorities are targeting the start of construction next year and mass production in 2030. This means that if demand remains strong in the coming years, equipment deliveries to the planned facilities could face bottlenecks.
Against the backdrop, ASML Chief Financial Officer Roger Dassen told analysts that ASML is holding off on accepting orders for 2029 and 2030 while it assesses both customers' readiness and its own ability to meet future demand.
"We don't want now to accept orders from customer A, B and C and then to tell customer D, who hasn't given orders yet for 2029 and 2030, 'Sorry, we're sold out,'" Dassen told analysts on the post-earnings call.
“While policy support for the Jeonnam-Gwangju clusters has largely focused on speeding up land development and power supply, securing equipment could emerge as a new variable in how quickly the fabs come online,” another industry official said.

articles.title: India’s GDP growth set to break 20-year record, South Korean economist explains why - News9live
articles.summary: India’s GDP growth set to break 20-year record, South Korean economist explains why  News9live
articles.full_text:
India's economy could be approaching its longest period of sustained growth above 7 per cent, according to South Korean economist Kyunghoon Kim. His analysis shows that India's average annual GDP growth during 2021-2025 reached 7.83 per cent, the second-highest five-year average since 1960. With the IMF, World Bank and ADB raising their forecasts, India could surpass its previous growth streak recorded between 2003 and 2007.
Kim’s analysis comes as the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank and Asian Development Bank (ADB) project growth of around 7 per cent or higher for India. According to the economist, India has recorded five consecutive calendar years of growth above 7 per cent, matching its performance between 2003 and 2007. If the latest forecasts materialise, the country could break that earlier record.
Nearly all major forecasters, including the IMF, ADB and World Bank, have recently raised their growth forecasts for India to above 7% for this year AND next. Remarkable in itself – even more so when viewed against India’s recent performance. (1/n) https://t.co/3xfQdPvEsY
— Kyunghoon Kim (@Kyunghoon_Kim_) October 16, 2026
India could surpass its 2003-2007 growth streak
India’s economy contracted by 5.8 per cent during the pandemic in 2020 before rebounding by 9.7 per cent in 2021, according to figures shared by Kim.
It subsequently grew by more than 7 per cent in each of the following four years.
“That makes five consecutive years of growth above 7%, matching the 2003–2007 run, when India attracted global attention as one of the BRIC economies,” Kim wrote on X.
He added that India would surpass that streak if current forecasts hold.
The comparison is significant. The 2003-2007 period was one of India’s strongest phases of sustained economic expansion, when the country attracted growing international investor interest.
India’s post-pandemic growth is close to a historic high
Kim highlighted another statistic that puts India’s recent performance into perspective.
According to his calculations, India’s average annual growth between 2021 and 2025 was 7.83 per cent, compared with 7.89 per cent during 2003-2007.
That makes the latest five-year period the second-strongest in the historical series dating back to 1960.
“Sustaining such momentum over several years deserves attention,” Kim wrote.
The figures suggest that India’s recent economic expansion extends well beyond the immediate recovery following the pandemic.
IMF, World Bank and ADB raise India’s growth forecasts
Kim’s thread highlighted how major international institutions have become more optimistic about India’s economic performance.
The IMF recently raised India’s growth forecast for 2026-27 from 6.4 per cent to 7 per cent. It expects another 7 per cent expansion in 2027-28, according to its October World Economic Outlook.
“Many economists, myself included, repeatedly revised forecasts upwards as quarterly GDP figures came in,” Kim wrote.
His charts show the World Bank, IMF and ADB lifting their projections, with recent estimates clustering around or above 7 per cent.
The upgrades are significant amid concerns about high global energy prices, geopolitical tensions and slower economic growth in several major economies.
A 7 per cent growth rate means much more for India today
Kim pointed out that India’s economy has grown substantially since its previous high-growth period.
In 2007, India’s GDP was just above $1 trillion. Today, it is approaching $4 trillion, according to the figures he shared.
That means a 7 per cent growth rate now represents a much larger increase in economic output than the same percentage did nearly two decades ago.
“The same 7% growth rate therefore represents a much larger expansion,” Kim explained.
He expects India to become the world’s third-largest economy around 2030, though such rankings depend on exchange rates, inflation and the performance of other countries.
India’s performance deserves attention
A sustained growth rate above 7 per cent would be a significant achievement for an economy with a population of around 140 crore.
Yet headline GDP growth does not automatically mean equal improvements in household incomes, employment opportunities or living standards.
The pace of job creation, private investment and income growth will remain important measures of how broadly the benefits reach Indian households.
Kim acknowledged the challenges but argued that India’s performance deserves greater international recognition.
“Many challenges remain, but this economic performance of a country of 1.4 billion people deserves celebration,” he wrote.
He ended his thread on an optimistic note, expressing hope that future quarterly GDP releases would give economists further reasons to revise their forecasts upwards.

articles.summary: Kospi rebounds over 2% on eased chip rout, Fed bets  Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.full_text:
Trade volume was light at 286.5 million shares worth 20 trillion won ($15 billion). Winners far outnumbered losers 757 to 134.
Investors went bargain hunting for large-cap tech shares, particularly the country's top chipmakers, which tumbled over 10 percent the previous session.
Foreigners were net buyers, snapping up 343.5 billion won worth of stocks, while retail and institutional investors offloaded a combined net 1.17 trillion won.
During the 2026 IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh voiced optimism for the U.S. economy and its strength while he refrained from signaling whether there will be a rate hike this month.
Warsh's comments revived appetite for risky assets as a series of recent U.S. inflation data signaled that prices are rising at a faster pace than expected.
Investor sentiment was also lifted by the Fed chair's expression of optimism for AI, which he described as "probably the most consequential change to the U.S. and the global economy in my lifetime."
"It is meaningful that the Fed Chair maintained a positive assessment of the AI industry's structural growth, despite concerns over growing credit risks and funding burdens at such companies," Seo Sang-yong, an analyst at Mirae Asset Securities, said.
Comments from Nvidia chief Jensen Huang also helped elevate financial health concerns over the AI industry as well. On Thursday, Huang expressed optimism for its partner cloud company, CoreWeave, saying the firms' financial strength is "improving every day."
Shares of CoreWeave slid over 15 percent Wednesday after a dramatic spike in its corporate bond yields of near 15 percent triggered investor anxiety over the company's heavy AI-related debt burden.
In Seoul, most market heavyweights closed higher.
Semiconductor giant Samsung Electronics was up 2.62 percent to 215,500 won, while industry rival SK hynix inched up 0.79 percent to 1,272,000 won.
Carmaker Hyundai Motor added 5.58 percent to 312,000 won, defense giant Hanwha Aerospace advanced 7.77 percent to 888,000 won, and bio firm Celltrion climbed 6.53 percent to 194,000 won.
The Korean won weakened by 13.2 won against the U.S. dollar, trading at 1,331.4 won as of 3:30 p.m.

articles.full_text:
16 Oct 2026 , 01:05 PM
Asian stock markets sold off on Thursday, following strong US inflation data which raised concerns that the Federal Reserve would keep interest rates higher for longer. South Korea’s KOSPI fell 7.57% on Thursday, October 15, while Taiwan’s market saw a reported record single-day outflow of NT$302.5 billion, equivalent to approximately $9.3 billion.
Technology and semiconductor shares led the fall which temporarily paused a major market in South Korea as losses accumulated during the session.
South Korea Stock Market: KOSPI Falls 7.57%
South Korea’s benchmark KOSPI index dropped 454.59 points to close at 5,554.22. The index had fallen up to 9.29% intraday which led to a 20 minute pause in trading.
The index hit a new losing streak of seven consecutive sessions as it reached a six month low. The pause in South Korea’s markets was reportedly the 10th for the index this year.

|---|---|
| KOSPI closing level | 5,554.22 | 
| Point decline | 454.59 | 
| Closing decline | 7.57% | 
| Maximum intraday decline | 9.29% | 
| Trading halt | 20 minutes | 
| Foreign investor net selling | 3.6 trillion won | 
| Korean won exchange rate | 1,344.6 per US dollar | 
South Korea-based foreign investors sold shares valued at 3.6 trillion won or around $2.68 billion.
Semiconductor shares saw some of the biggest losses as concerns about US interests rates and spending on artificial intelligence (AI) took the technology stocks down.
| Stock or indicator | Decline | 
|---|---|
| Samsung Electronics | 9.5% | 
| SK Hynix | 11.1% | 
| LG Energy Solution | 4.6% | 
| Hyundai Motor | 5.7% | 
| Philadelphia Semiconductor Index | 4.3% overnight | 
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix shares were big contributors on South Korea’s markets after the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index saw a 4.3% overnight fall. The fall in technology shares reflects concerns that the large sums going into AI infrastructure will lead to earnings growth at a pace that supports valuations. Increasing interest rates can decrease the present value investors apply to earnings, especially with technology stocks. Of the 917 South Korean stocks traded during the session, 789 were down and 113 up indicating that a decline was not limited to some big technology stocks.
Taiwan’s stock market also experienced a sell-off as it fell more than 1,600 points as a result of foreign investors reportedly seeing a net sale of NT$302.5 billion, or approximately $9.3 billion in a single day. The outflow placed further pressure on a market that is well exposed to the semiconductor manufacturing and global technology sector. Domestic investors, however, took the opposite approach and grew their exposure to exchange-traded funds (ETFs).
Yuantai Taiwan 50 ETF (0050) recorded a reported record NT$37.8 billion in net subscriptions. The Yuanta Taiwan 50 Daily Leveraged 2X ETF (00631L) attracted NT$11.9 billion in inflows to reach its largest daily inflow in six months. The move suggests that some domestic investors believed the steep drop could be an opportunity to add exposure to the market. However, inflows to ETFs do not mean that the market is close to a bottom.Leveraged ETFs also have more risk as they look to enhance daily index moves but can see large losses when the market falls day after day and fail to capture twice the rise of a given index when it moves upward.
The selling reflects concerns about US inflation, interest rates and technology sector valuations.
1. Higher US inflation raises rate concerns
Stronger than expected US Consumer Price Index led to concerns that inflation could remain persistent and that inflation could keep the Federal Reserve from loosening its interest rate policy for a longer period of time. Higher rates can increase financing costs to businesses and can make equities less attractive compared to interest instruments.
2. Semiconductor stocks face valuation pressure
South Korea and Taiwan have a big exposure to the global semiconductor industry. Semiconductor stocks can see large share-price moves when investors start to reconsider the outlook for spending on technology. Concerns over the sustainability of AI spending have added to the uncertainty, particularly with those companies with valuations that appear to be built on continued increases in data centres, advanced chips and related infrastructure.
3. Foreign investor selling intensifies declines
The reported outflows from South Korea and Taiwan from foreign investors added further pressure to already struggling markets. Large selling activity can add to declines in markets, particularly when focused on major constituents. However, the direction of the market is not just driven by foreign fund flows. There are several other factors that affect performance, including domestic demand, company earnings, movement in currency and economic conditions.
Some analysts have pointed to long term growth prospects and a potential rebound after a strong decline. Historical prices cited in the supplied report show that the Taiwan 50 Index rose between 24.3% and 147.3% in the six months after each of four previous significant sell-offs. Those examples are not a guarantee that the same will happen now and the size and length of a rebound will vary depending on the circumstances surrounding the sell-off. In South Korea, financial authorities reportedly held an emergency meeting and pledged to respond in a proactive manner to support the market and protect investors. However, the effectiveness of any measures will be tested against the conditions surrounding the situation.
The next directions in Asian markets will be partly driven by whether US inflation and interest rate expectations stabilize. Investors will also turn to the semiconductor earnings, updated spending on AI and movement in funds as well as foreign fund flows. For South Korea and Taiwan, the big concentration on their stock markets on technology and semiconductor companies makes the outlook on global chip demand all the more important. The big fall in South Korea’s stock market and Taiwan’s domestic ETF inflows show two different approaches by investors in response to a common set of market developments. Neither is a sure indicator of what will happen in the future.

[News] Korean Chip Engineer Accuses Tesla of Pressuring Samsung on AI5/AI6 Pricing, Poaching Talent for Terafab
A South Korean semiconductor engineer has accused Tesla of imposing unfair contract terms on Samsung and Elon Musk’s Terafab project of poaching talent from the chipmaker’s Texas facility. According to Wccftech, the engineer, who uses the X handle @TTHUEONE, claimed that Tesla demanded access to Samsung’s internal fab information and audit rights for its AI5 and AI6 chip contracts while aggressively pushing down foundry prices. The engineer also alleged that Terafab had poached numerous employees from Samsung’s Taylor fab in Texas and that Tesla turned to Samsung Foundry for its AI5 and AI6 chips because TSMC wouldn’t meet its demands.
The accusations followed Musk’s recent comments on memory chip pricing. Earlier this week, Musk praised Micron, saying the company “has been reasonable regarding future memory prices, while others have been extortionate,” in remarks widely interpreted as criticism of Samsung, Wccftech notes.
Terafab Raises Talent and Technology Concerns for Samsung
The allegations echo concerns raised in March by South Korean outlet Business Post, which warned that Terafab could intensify competition with Samsung for semiconductor talent and equipment. With its planned site just a 30-minute drive from Samsung’s Taylor foundry, Terafab could tap into the same regional workforce and supplier network, the report noted. Tesla had already begun recruiting semiconductor development engineers for the project.
More recently, Financial News reported on October 12 that Samsung has begun deploying advanced-node yield engineers from South Korea to its Taylor facility while expanding local recruitment ahead of planned 2nm mass production in 2027. The company aims to begin operating the fab by the end of 2026, with Tesla among its key customers. Separately, Seoul Economic Daily reported in September that Samsung had begun trial production of Tesla’s AI5 chips at the facility, with yield verification underway ahead of full-scale production in 2027.
Business Post also flagged potential risks to Samsung’s intellectual property and manufacturing know-how. The report highlighted Musk’s direct involvement in AI6 chip production, including plans for a private office at Samsung’s Taylor facility, suggesting that such access could provide insights into Samsung’s 2nm operations that might benefit Terafab’s development.
Tesla Orders and TSMC’s Potential Role in Terafab
Tesla remains a key customer for Samsung’s foundry business. According to an earlier report by South Korea’s AsiaToday, Tesla’s AI5 and AI6 chip orders are expected to support initial capacity utilization at Samsung’s Taylor fab. The report also noted that TSMC’s potential involvement in Terafab could complicate Samsung’s efforts to secure future chip orders.
Meanwhile, TSMC Chairman C.C. Wei confirmed that the company is in discussions over Terafab, though the outcome remains uncertain. He emphasized that any fab involving TSMC would have to be operated by the company itself. This contrasts with Musk’s position on October 7, when he said his companies would build and operate Terafab, with TSMC potentially subleasing part of the facility rather than taking an operational role, according to Reuters.

articles.title: Korea leverage ban shifts retail into index ETFs and margin, amplifying crash - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
articles.summary: Korea leverage ban shifts retail into index ETFs and margin, amplifying crash - CHOSUNBIZ  Chosunbiz
articles.full_text:
Single-stock leveraged exchange-traded funds (ETFs), long singled out as the main culprits behind the market's sharp swings, came under regulation at the end of July, but KOSPI's plunge has not eased this month. Since the regulation, trading value in single-stock leveraged ETFs has fallen 95%, making their direct impact on the index negligible, but it appears a "balloon effect" has emerged as retail investors' demand for leverage has shifted to index-leveraged ETFs or margin financing.
On the 16th, the KOSPI index was tallied to have fallen 18.7% over 10 trading days this month. The previous day, on the 15th, the KOSPI index closed down 7.57% at 5,554.22, marking a seventh straight session of declines. It was also the steepest drop since July 28 (-10.84%).
Although the market's roller-coaster pattern has intensified in October, the ripple effect of single-stock leveraged ETFs in the latest whipsaw appears limited. On the previous day, when losses were steep, the 16 single-stock leveraged ETFs posted 803.7 billion won in trading value. The October daily average trading value was around 561 billion won.
Compared with the average trading value of 12.2735 trillion won from July 1–30, before financial authorities implemented the single-stock leveraged ETF curbs, the figure is down about 95%.
Compared with the Korea Exchange main board's trading value, it is clear that trading in single-stock leveraged ETFs has shrunk sharply. The previous day, single-stock leveraged ETFs accounted for 2.81% of the main board's total trading value, and the October daily average share also stayed around 2.5%. Compared with July (33.8%), before the curbs took effect, it has shriveled to about one-twelfth.
That does not mean retail investors' appetite for leverage itself has waned. A "balloon effect" has emerged as funds have shifted to index-leveraged ETFs and margin financing to skirt the single-stock rules.
According to Koscom ETF Check, over the past week the No. 1 net buy by retail investors among ETFs was KODEX Leverage (670.1 billion won). No. 4 was KODEX KOSDAQ150 Leverage (251.9 billion won), No. 7 was KODEX Semiconductor Leverage (108.1 billion won), and No. 10 was TIGER Semiconductor TOP10 Leverage (71.5 billion won). Retail investors' purchases of these four products accounted for 51% of the top 10 net buys.
The shift to "bit-too" ("borrowing to invest") is also clear. Outstanding margin financing, which had increased to 38 trillion won in June, fell to the 27 trillion won range in August. It then began to rise again, and from the 2nd to the 14th, during the sharp decline when the KOSPI index fell 14.2%, outstanding margin financing increased to 33.7057 trillion won.
Ultimately, in the domestic market's distorted structure concentrated in large semiconductor stocks such as Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, observers say volatility is being amplified, making it especially vulnerable to bad news, as retail investors' high-risk leverage sentiment piles on.
Lee Sang-heon, Director General of the iM Securities Research Center, said, "The domestic market rose sharply on the boom in semiconductor stocks, but as credit risks at global artificial intelligence (AI) companies have surfaced recently, concerns have grown over a slowdown in semiconductor investment, and the market has taken a big hit from that," adding, "Japan's market fell less than Korea's because its weighting in semiconductor stocks is not high."

Icheon City Operates Investment Promotion Booth at SEDEX 2026
Expands Business Engagement After Three Consecutive Years of Participation
Highlights Seoul Metropolitan Area Accessibility and Semiconductor Industry Base
Encourages New Investment Through Tailored Consultations
Icheon City in Gyeonggi Province has taken part in South Korea’s largest exhibition specializing in semiconductors to attract semiconductor companies. The city’s strategy is to attract new investments and companies looking to relocate by highlighting its accessibility from the Seoul metropolitan area and its established semiconductor industry base.
Icheon City is promoting its investment environment and industrial competitiveness to domestic and international semiconductor industry officials at an investment promotion booth at the 28th Semiconductor Exhibition (SEDEX 2026), held at COEX in Seoul from the 14th to 16th. Icheon City said on October 16 that it had taken part in the 28th Semiconductor Expo (SEDEX 2026), held at COEX in Seoul from October 14 to 16, and conducted investment promotion activities targeting semiconductor companies from South Korea and abroad.
A total of 300 companies, including Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, participated in this year’s event, which drew about 60,000 visitors.

China and North Korea officially marked the long-delayed opening of their most significant land border crossing on Thursday, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce after years of soured ties and pandemic-related disruptions to cross-border exchange.
The 3-km (2-mile) New Yalu River Bridge and the Chinese customs at the end of the 1.3-km crossing saw increased activity over the past few days, with trucks adorned with Chinese flags waiting on the bridge ahead of a crossing on Thursday, Reuters reports.
Crowds also gathered on the Chinese side along a road overlooking the bridge.
Chinese and North Korean flags also lined the cable-stayed bridge with towering pylons that had been completed in 2014 but remained unused, while approach roads and a customs compound on the North Korea end remained unfinished.
On Thursday, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported the countries held an opening ceremony for the new bridge. North Korea's state media have yet to report on the scheduled event.
The opening signals progress in bilateral relations between Beijing and Pyongyang, marked by two summit meetings between their leaders in the past year.
China is by far Pyongyang's largest trading partner, even after a series of UN sanctions banned the flow of goods and workers to and from North Korea over the country's defiant missile and nuclear weapons development.
China and Russia, two UN Security Council permanent member states that voted to approve sanctions resolutions until 2017, have since questioned the legitimacy and efficacy of such bans.
Analysts said North Korea, despite the potential economic boost from active trade, remains cautious of greater dependence on China. Russia is accused by countries such as the US and South Korea of supplying sensitive military assistance to the North in return for Pyongyang's helpin fighting the war in Ukraine.
"The bridge is unlikely to lead immediately to a full-scale return to pre-sanctions trade," said Lim Eul-chul at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies.
But the bridge will help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products needed for North Korea's development projects, he said.

Bangkok – A senior International Monetary Fund official has expressed his support for Japan’s plan to lower the consumption tax on food as a temporary measure to address soaring prices.
With Japan also planning to introduce a benefit program linked to income levels, Rahul Anand, IMF assistant director and mission chief for Japan, said the approach was “a very welcome step.”
Still, he warned against fiscal deterioration, noting that Japan’s debt level is exceptionally high compared with those of other major economies.
On Oct. 9, the Japanese government adopted a bill to lower the 8% consumption tax rate for food items to 1% for two years beginning in April next year and introduce the benefit program targeting low- and middle-income workers.
The Lower House is slated to begin deliberation on the bill Tuesday.
“The other thing that’s also very encouraging is the announcement by the (Japanese) authorities that they are not going to issue additional debt to finance this consumption tax (cut) bill,” Anand said.
The best way to support households adversely affected by a higher cost of living is through “targeted, temporary and also budget-neutral” measures, given Japan’s very high level of debt, he added.
As for the rise in long-term interest rates, there are concerns about an increase in debt repayment costs.
With Japan’s social security spending expected to continue growing, Anand said, “it is important to build buffers,” while maintaining the downward trend in its debt-to-GDP (gross domestic product) ratio.
On interest rate hikes by the Bank of Japan, Anand said, “Given such high uncertainties, we think that the BOJ is very appropriately conducting monetary policy.”
He said that if the yen weakens further and leads to higher inflation, the BOJ would need to raise its policy rate. He also projected that the inflation rate in Japan would rise over the next few months and then decline toward the BOJ’s 2% target by the end of next year.

Analysis suggests that the Bank of Korea’s hawkish monetary policy stance has widened the decline in the Korean stock market during sharp sell-offs. The argument is that a rate-hiking trend increases corporate interest burdens and drags down equity valuations. While the domestic stock market has exhibited a ‘RollerKOSPI’ (roller coaster + KOSPI) pattern this year, the KOSPI index’s gain has been only half that of the Taiwan Weighted Index, the representative benchmark for the Taiwanese stock market.
According to financial investment industry sources on the 17th, the KOSPI index closed at 5,554.22 on the 15th, up 31.80% from the end of last year. Over the same period, the Taiwan Weighted Index rose 62.17% to 46,969.87. The U.S. S&P 500 index stood at 7,744.06 on the 15th (local time), up 13.13% from the end of last year, while the NASDAQ index climbed 14.93% to 26,713.03. Japan’s Nikkei 225 index rose 27.98% from the end of last year to 64,425.95 on the same day.
The KOSPI fell by as much as 7.57% on the 15th. On the same day, the Taiwan Weighted Index dropped 3.41%, meaning the KOSPI’s decline was more than double that of the Taiwan Weighted Index.
The backdrop for the sharp drop in the KOSPI index was the outflow of foreign capital. Foreign investors made net sales worth 3.7659 trillion won on the KOSPI that day. Retail investors and institutional investors made net purchases worth 1.4381 trillion won and 1.6747 trillion won, respectively. The reasons cited for the foreign investor exodus include rising global long-term interest rates and concerns over a slowdown in artificial intelligence (AI) investment.
Market observers predict that as the Bank of Korea intensifies its tightening moves, the Korean stock market faces an increased likelihood of stronger downward pressure compared to major economies. High interest rates increase corporate interest burdens and weigh on equity valuations, which are calculated by discounting future earnings to present value.
In fact, NH Investment & Securities diagnosed that the reason the Korean stock market has been hit harder than Taiwan is “because the Bank of Korea is particularly hawkish.” NH Investment & Securities expects the Bank of Korea to pursue additional rate hikes, given its forecast of 3.5% for next year’s Korean economic growth rate. However, it noted that there may be room to adjust the policy stance if fears regarding stock market and corporate debt repayment risks grow.
Bank of Korea Governor Shin Hyun-song explained during the national audit on the 12th that he raised the base rate consecutively in July and August to preemptively curb the spread of inflation and respond to financial stability risks.
Taiwan’s monetary policy environment is different. The Central Bank of Taiwan froze its policy rate for the 10th consecutive time on the 17th of last month (local time). The consumer price inflation forecast presented by the Central Bank of Taiwan for this year is 2.03%.
Semiconductor stocks, a key sector in the stock market, also showed differing downside support during the sharp decline. On the 15th, TSMC fell only 2.01%, while Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix plunged 9.48% and 11.06%, respectively. It appears that the differing conditions each company faces in the semiconductor sector have been reflected in stock prices alongside industry outlooks.
TSMC is the world’s largest company in the foundry (semiconductor contract manufacturing) field, which involves producing semiconductors based on designs by clients. In contrast, memory semiconductors, the mainstay of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, are produced and sold by a few companies with similar products, causing prices to fluctuate significantly according to supply and demand; an increase in competitors leads to downward price pressure.
The Japanese and U.S. stock markets also carry concerns over AI investment returns and additional U.S. rate hikes. However, on the 15th (local time), the New York stock market saw government bond yields fall and buying concentrate in consumer stocks, pushing the Dow Jones Industrial Average up 1.08% from the previous day to 52,177.69. The NASDAQ index’s gain was limited to 0.08%. Weakness in AI-related stocks was partially offset by gains in other sectors.
NH Investment & Securities predicts that while the domestic stock market may need time to find direction due to regulatory concerns surrounding the U.S. midterm elections, it could rebound after confirming a bottom twice once supply and demand pressures ease.

Bank of Japan (BoJ) Governor Kazuo Ueda reiterated on Friday that the central bank will continue raising interest rates as underlying inflation approaches its 2% target, noting that financial conditions remain accommodative.
Ueda said economic activity and price developments remain broadly in line with the BoJ's forecasts, while policymakers will discuss at their upcoming meeting whether to revise their assessment of underlying inflation. He added that the timing and pace of future rate hikes will depend on the impact of exchange rate movements, Artificial Intelligence (AI) demand and developments in the Middle East on prices.
The BoJ Governor also highlighted that some global policymakers appeared more optimistic about AI-driven demand than the Japanese central bank had anticipated, although discussions this week did not materially alter its baseline economic outlook.
No big gap in view between what we have assessed on inflationary pressure from AI demand, and what I heard from global policymakers.
I felt that there were more policymakers at this meeting who were somewhat more bullish on ai-demand than we had estimated.
We will continue to raise interest rates as underlying inflation approaching 2%, financial conditions are accommodative.
Economic, price moves roughly in LINE with our forecasts.
Did not hear anything at this week's meetings that deviated from our baseline view.
We will discuss at upcoming meeting whether to tweak our assessment that underlying inflation is approaching 2%.
Timing, pace of future rate hikes will be decided looking at impact of fx, AI demand and Middle East developments on prices.
Haven't been in touch with us treasury secretary bessent since we met in asheville.
As underlying inflation is quite close to 2%, it is becoming more important than before to anchor inflation around our target.
Ueda's remarks had little impact on financial markets, with USD/JPY hovering around 157.95 at the time of writing, virtually unchanged on Friday.
The Bank of Japan (BoJ) is the Japanese central bank, which sets monetary policy in the country. Its mandate is to issue banknotes and carry out currency and monetary control to ensure price stability, which means an inflation target of around 2%.
The Bank of Japan embarked in an ultra-loose monetary policy in 2013 in order to stimulate the economy and fuel inflation amid a low-inflationary environment. The bank’s policy is based on Quantitative and Qualitative Easing (QQE), or printing notes to buy assets such as government or corporate bonds to provide liquidity. In 2016, the bank doubled down on its strategy and further loosened policy by first introducing negative interest rates and then directly controlling the yield of its 10-year government bonds. In March 2024, the BoJ lifted interest rates, effectively retreating from the ultra-loose monetary policy stance.
The Bank’s massive stimulus caused the Yen to depreciate against its main currency peers. This process exacerbated in 2022 and 2023 due to an increasing policy divergence between the Bank of Japan and other main central banks, which opted to increase interest rates sharply to fight decades-high levels of inflation. The BoJ’s policy led to a widening differential with other currencies, dragging down the value of the Yen. This trend partly reversed in 2024, when the BoJ decided to abandon its ultra-loose policy stance.
A weaker Yen and the spike in global energy prices led to an increase in Japanese inflation, which exceeded the BoJ’s 2% target. The prospect of rising salaries in the country – a key element fuelling inflation – also contributed to the move.

articles.full_text:
For months, a simple market axiom held sway: whenever tech giants pledged ever-larger sums for data centers and graphics processors, chipmaker valuations climbed without resistance. That logic cracked this October week.
Advanced Micro Devices is absorbing the shift in full. The stock traded at EUR 493.20 in today's session, down 1.6%, though it still boasts a hefty 168% gain year-to-date. The pullback follows Thursday's close of EUR 501.40, when the shares tested a key support line before the retreat resumed into the weekend.
When the Customers' Balance Sheets Start to Creak
The source of the latest unease sits not in the chipmakers' fabs but in their clients' finances. When credit default swap premiums for AI data center operator CoreWeave spiked and its bonds came under strain, skepticism spread across the entire sector. Baird analyst Mortonson captured the mood: Wall Street is growing weary of the quasi-financing model run by companies like Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom. Rising capital costs and circular funding structures are eroding confidence.
The warning signs are hard to miss. With neocloud providers groaning under heavy interest burdens—and Gartner projections suggesting more than 80% of these operators could cease independent operations by 2030—fears of order cuts are mounting. Chipmakers like AMD no longer sell into a market of unlimited budgets; they must watch customers measure spending plans against the reality of expensive credit.
Lisa Su's Answer: Lock Down the Supply Chain
AMD CEO Lisa Su is responding on the technology front. She named South Korean tech giants Samsung Electronics and SK hynix as key partners for the company's data center ambitions, according to Reuters. Discussions include expanding deliveries of advanced HBM4 memory for AMD's upcoming Instinct MI455X accelerator generation, along with options for deeper collaboration in contract manufacturing.
Those tie-ups carry strategic weight, since high-bandwidth memory ranks among the most critical components for AI accelerators. Earlier in the week, at the OCP Global Summit, AMD also unveiled its open reference architecture Helion for agentic AI data centers. The design supports configurations with up to 32,768 processor cores and aims to set specifications for the next generation of large-scale IT infrastructure.
Solid Fundamentals Against the Credit Fears
AMD's core business, meanwhile, has been remarkably strong. In the second quarter of 2026, revenue climbed to a record USD 11.5 billion, driven largely by a doubling of Data Center segment revenue to USD 6.7 billion. Management is targeting roughly USD 13.0 billion for the third quarter. Technological announcements such as Helios, the MI400 series and an agreement with Anthropic covering up to two gigawatts of MI450 graphics processors show AMD keeping pace in the race for top-tier hardware.
Even the strongest balance sheet offers only limited shelter from macroeconomic currents. Freshly stoked U.S. inflation concerns and the specter of further rate hikes hit capital-intensive industries hard. If borrowed capital stays expensive, customers grow less willing to advance billions for new server clusters on credit.
A Sector-Wide Repricing
Reuters reported that U.S. semiconductor stocks recently came under notable selling pressure, triggered by bets on rising rates and growing doubts about the sustainability of billion-dollar data center spending. AMD could not escape the broad industry downturn. Reports of revised revenue forecasts from individual AI players, combined with hot U.S. inflation data, had already dampened market risk appetite.
For AMD, this moment marks a turning point in the current semiconductor cycle. The company has proven convincingly that it can deliver first-class silicon solutions. Whether its valuation can defend its high level over the coming months will hinge not solely on the computing power of new graphics processors, but on the financial viability of the customers who operate them.
The company has said it will report third-quarter 2026 results on November 3 after the U.S. market close. Until then, the share price is likely to be driven largely by broader sentiment in the semiconductor sector and further signals on global data center utilization.

The global sell-off in technology stocks continued on Thursday. In the U.S. markets, NVIDIA closed down 1.84%, AMD fell 1.5%, Intel dropped about 2.8%, and Dell Technologies plunged 6.8%. Asian markets suffered even steeper losses, with SK Hynix plunging over 10% in a single day, Samsung Electronics falling 8.73%, and Japan’s SoftBank Group sliding 7.9%.
Article author and source: Wall Street Journal
Expectations of interest rate hikes, rising financing costs for AI, and a deteriorating competitive landscape converged this week, triggering a broad sell-off in global tech stocks.
The global sell-off in technology stocks continued on Thursday. In the U.S. markets, NVIDIA closed down 1.84%, AMD fell 1.5%, Intel dropped about 2.8%, and Dell Technologies plunged 6.8%. Asian markets suffered even steeper losses, with SK Hynix plunging over 10% in a single day, Samsung Electronics falling 8.73%, and Japan’s SoftBank Group sliding 7.9%.
According to CNBC, as of Thursday this week, the combined market value of the world’s top 20 AI and semiconductor stocks has declined by over $1 trillion. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX), which tracks the chip sector, recorded its eighth consecutive day of declines on Thursday, with a cumulative drop of approximately 12.7% during the period—marking the longest consecutive losing streak in the ETF’s 11-year history, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang told Bloomberg during an event in Stockholm that he believes NVIDIA does not need to endorse CoreWeave, adding that "their cost of capital is actually declining." This comment spurred a intraday rebound in neocloud stocks, with CoreWeave closing up 5.94% and Nebius rising 1.29%.
Multiple negative factors are overlapping, creating a layered selling logic. This selling pressure is not triggered by a single event, but rather by multiple negative catalysts reinforcing each other within the same time frame.
Inflation data was the trigger. The U.S. September Consumer Price Index (CPI), released on Wednesday, came in higher than expected, prompting the market to increase bets on further Fed rate hikes. The Nasdaq Composite closed down 1.88% at 26,692.87, while the S&P 500 fell 1.11% to 7,718.94.
Anthropic’s data has further weighed on market sentiment. According to the Financial Times, the AI startup Anthropic disclosed at a private investor meeting on Wednesday that its third-quarter revenue reached $16.8 billion, a roughly 50% quarter-over-quarter increase—but this growth rate was far below the approximately 145% quarter-over-quarter increase seen in the second quarter. D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria wrote in a client report: "The market appears to have interpreted Anthropic’s update as a negative signal, which is understandable given the market’s heightened sensitivity to AI-related trading."
Luria himself holds a more neutral view on this. He noted that Anthropic generated positive cash flow in the third quarter, indicating that the company and OpenAI "are not inherently unprofitable business models." He also wrote that, from a broader perspective of the AI industry, "overall AI usage (and AI spending) does not necessarily show signs of slowing down."
Competition in China is intensifying. Last weekend, CXMT announced a breakthrough in a new architecture that enables more data to be stored in a smaller space. Elon Musk then posted on X that China will produce "massive amounts of memory chips" by 2028.
Meanwhile, the CEOs of Broadcom and Intel both warned on Monday that financing issues could become a major obstacle to AI expansion, with Broadcom CEO Hock Tan stating that this challenge could even surpass shortages of chips or power.
Rising interest rates directly impact the return on investment for AI infrastructure, and this effect of high interest rates on AI infrastructure development is one of the core rationales behind this sell-off.
James Vrachas, Executive Director at investment bank Post Oak Group, told MarketWatch that chip stocks have "already priced in a large portion of future growth expectations," with their current prices reflecting those forecasts. Under these conditions, "even a slight shift in sentiment or questioning of spending could have a significant impact on stock prices." He added, "Believing in the long-term potential of AI is different from believing that every company benefiting from this growth is fairly valued."
Baird investment strategist Ross Mayfield told MarketWatch that rising Treasury yields are pressuring the chip sector, particularly high-growth stocks and companies on the more aggressive end of the AI risk spectrum that rely heavily on external financing. He noted that CPI data could heighten the urgency for the Fed to raise rates, "creating significant pressure on short-term interest rates and directly impacting borrowers with weaker financial fundamentals or floating-rate debt tied to short-term rates."
Mayfield also noted that even hyperscalers are not entirely immune to interest rate changes. "Even the largest and most cash-rich companies must reassess the return on investment for these projects," he said, "and since much of the market's momentum is built on hyperscalers' spending on hardware and data center infrastructure, this casts a shadow over the entire supply chain."
Markets in Asia and Europe experienced deeper declines, with South Korean and Japanese stocks hit hardest. The selling sentiment from U.S. markets rapidly spread to Asia and Europe, where losses generally exceeded those in the U.S.
On Thursday, South Korea’s SK Hynix plunged over 10% in a single day, Samsung Electronics fell 8.73%, LG Innotek dropped 8.95%, Seoul Semiconductor declined 9.28%, and Samsung SDI slid 6.26%. The Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) neared its lowest closing level since April.
The Japanese market also suffered heavy losses. SoftBank Group fell 7.9%, Advantest, a semiconductor test equipment provider, plunged nearly 14%, Tokyo Electron, a chip manufacturing equipment supplier, dropped 6.45%, and Renesas Electronics declined 8%. TSMC fell 1.81%.
In Europe, Dutch semiconductor equipment giant ASML slipped slightly, Infineon fell 5%, and ASM International dropped 7%.
Analyst: Demand signals are the true alarm line; despite weak market sentiment, some analysts believe this selling pressure has not yet reached a material deterioration in AI demand.
Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives wrote in a report that this sell-off reflects market concerns over financing costs, not skepticism about demand for AI computing power. "The rise in U.S. Treasury yields above 5% has indeed increased financing costs for these infrastructure projects; it is reasonable for investors to focus on balance sheets and contract structures, but interest rates are a financing issue, not a demand issue."
Ives believes the current moment presents a buying opportunity and states that the AI infrastructure boom is still in its early stages. He clearly identifies the true warning signs to watch for: "What would actually change our assessment are demand signals, not interest rate signals"—including hyperscale cloud providers cutting capital expenditure plans, contract cancellations, or declining GPU rental prices.
Gabelli Funds portfolio manager Hendi Susanto told MarketWatch that many chip and semiconductor equipment companies "have remained financially strong with ample free cash flow," and he expects most of them to "end the year on a strong note," particularly those where demand still outstrips supply. He also noted that the upcoming earnings season for tech companies will reveal "the extent to which investors have priced in inflation concerns."

articles.title: Modi’s predicament: Gen Z pours out on India’s streets as dissent surges - The Japan Times
articles.summary: Modi’s predicament: Gen Z pours out on India’s streets as dissent surges  The Japan Times
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI – Despite tens of thousands of security personnel deployed to stop them, youth protesters in India scaled barricades last week, chanted anti-government slogans and scuffled with police officers trying to drag them away.
“Long live the revolution,” shouted one young man before police bundled him into a bus.
Street protests in India this year are likely to be higher than at any time in the past decade, the independent Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) Project has said, as dissent mounts against Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government and Gen Z activists pour on to the streets.
Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014, with people under 30 making up nearly one quarter of the country’s 1 billion voters. But his government remains stable and the next general election is not due until 2029.
“The nation has suddenly found its voice,” said Yogendra Yadav, an anti-government activist who has played a leading part in the demonstrations. “I would not say this is the beginning of the end of the Modi regime, but this definitely is the beginning of a downward spiral.”
The government and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party declined comment for this story.
The recent protests in the capital Delhi and elsewhere were focused on demands that Election Commission chief Gyanesh Kumar resign over a voter roll revision that activists and opposition parties say favours the BJP and has helped it win several recent state elections.
The ruling BJP, the government and the Election Commission deny the accusations. The BJP says the party’s wins have come from Modi’s popularity and strong economic growth.
But the demonstrations are also reflecting something larger: growing anger at Modi for failing to deliver jobs to millions of unemployed youth in his 12 years in power despite the surge in headline economic growth.
Other issues have also fed into the anti-establishment mood, including leaks of question papers in key examinations for jobs and education, the high number of crimes against women and the rise of billionaire businessmen alleged to have close links to Modi.
Modi has a strongman image and his government has previously cracked down on pockets of dissent harshly, but that hasn’t fazed the youngsters on the streets.
“The fear in us is gone,” said Ananya Raturi, a 21-year-old Delhi University student who was part of massive protests in the capital on Saturday.
Speaking after she clung to the windscreen wipers of a bus that police were using to detain protesters, Raturi said: “We don’t fear being detained or beaten up by the police. This generation enjoys it.”
Police have denied allegations that they beat up people at the demonstrations, saying protesters were handled according to prescribed procedures.
The rise of the cockroaches
The protests have been energized by the emergence of the first nationally resonant youth-led movement of the Modi era, the Cockroach Janta Party, which grew from online satire into a nationwide campaign this June after India’s chief justice likened the unemployed to “cockroaches.”
India’s mainstream media is mostly pro-government, critics say, and has covered the protests sparingly. But thousands of protesters armed with mobile phones as well as independent news channels on YouTube have amplified the unrest and made internet stars of leaders like CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and firebrand leftwing activist Neha Bora.
Opposition parties that were subdued under Modi’s grip on power have been reenergized, with Congress Party leader Rahul Gandhi and tens of thousands of followers also on the streets.
The unrest has drawn comparisons with neighboring Bangladesh and Nepal, where youth-led protest movements brought down governments in recent years, although analysts caution that India’s political landscape and Modi’s popularity make such parallels imperfect.
Many of the youth protesters grew up during Modi’s rise to power, buoyed by promises of jobs, opportunity and cleaner governance. A decade later, many say those aspirations remain unfulfilled and they say the Hindu nationalist government appears more focused on religious issues and divisive politics against minorities, especially Muslims.
The government has previously said the economy generated 168.3 million new jobs in the six years through 2024. Modi has repeatedly rejected allegations of any bias, saying his government works for all Indians.
30-year-old Gauri Seth, a medical student based in Kolkata, became a voter in 2014, the same year the Modi government came to power.
Seth said the Modi government promised “a lot, but has failed to deliver.”
“Instead they focus on things like religious infrastructure. There are cases of violence against minorities. When anyone speaks against them, it is labelled as treason or sedition.”
It’s mostly about jobs
When Modi came to power, he promised the creation of millions of jobs each year. Yet, despite India’s strong economic growth since then, unemployment remains at slightly above 5%, according to government data.
A Reuters poll last year said that data masks the severity of joblessness, especially among the youth. Unemployment among the 367 million people in the country aged 15-29 stood at 9.9% in 2025, according to the data.
Research by Azim Premji University’s State of Working India 2026 report found unemployment among graduates aged 15-25 was nearly 40%, while about one in five graduates aged 25-29 remained jobless.
In May, unrest erupted across the country when the government invalidated examinations for national medical colleges, a pathway to jobs for the poor and the middle class, after test papers were leaked.
Rubby Singh, a 30-year-old social activist in Delhi, said repeated examination paper leaks had deepened a sense among young Indians that the system was denying them opportunities even after years of study.
“This generation has been facing the brunt of not having proper education, which leads to not being able to get good opportunities,” she said.
While national elections are not due for almost three years, the country’s biggest state, Uttar Pradesh, goes to the polls early next year, which could provide a test of Modi’s popularity.
Analysts however remain cautious about the outcome.
The BJP may not be as strong as it was a few months ago, said Rahul Verma, a fellow at the Centre for Policy Research in New Delhi. “But whether there are going to be electoral implications, it is too early to say.”

articles.title: Freefall Without Wings: The Resurgence of the 'Korea Discount' - news.sbs.co.kr
articles.summary: Freefall Without Wings: The Resurgence of the 'Korea Discount'  news.sbs.co.kr
articles.full_text:
The stock market declined for seven consecutive trading days through yesterday (October 15). The KOSPI index, which had surpassed the 7,000-point mark, plummeted in a single breath to the 5,500 level. This week alone, selling sidecars were triggered twice and a circuit breaker once. Despite a modest rebound today (October 16), market anxiety remains pervasive. Global investment bank Goldman Sachs went as far as to state that this is "a far more serious phase than a typical short-term correction." Over the past 20 years, panic-selling episodes that wiped out 21% of the index across seven trading sessions occurred only twice: a 20.5% drop in March 2020 at the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, and a 15.1% drop in August 2011 during the downgrade of the U.S. sovereign credit rating. What lies behind this historic plunge?
① U.S. Inflation Rebound and Pressure from Delayed Rate Cuts
Higher-than-expected U.S. Consumer Price Index figures have reignited fears over prolonged high interest rates. An extended high-rate environment constricts global liquidity and stimulates risk-aversion sentiment toward assets such as emerging market equities.
② Resurfacing Doubts Over AI Profitability
Anxiety is mounting over investments in AI infrastructure, which had been driving valuations across global big tech and semiconductor sectors. Market doubts have flared up once again over whether real profit generation from AI infrastructure investments will materialize as swiftly as expected. As the possibility of big tech firms pacing their capital expenditures resurfaced, a share price correction was triggered across the entire global tech value chain.
③ Threat of Mid-to-Low-End Semiconductor Supply from China's CXMT and Others
Concerns have also emerged that the production yields and process migration speeds of Chinese memory makers, led by ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), are advancing faster than anticipated. In particular, CXMT's announcement that it aims to commercialize next-generation DRAM technology within this year dealt a direct blow. This heightened worries that an oversupply in the general-purpose DRAM market would sharply erode profit margins for South Korean chipmakers.
① Qualitative Differences in Memory Semiconductor Risk Exposure
The semiconductor sector accounts for half of the KOSPI index. Furthermore, compared to Taiwan, where TSMC holds a dominant foundry monopoly, or the United States, which centers on logic chips such as Intel and Qualcomm, South Korean chipmakers like Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix hold an overwhelming proportion in memory and commodity DRAM. Consequently, they are directly exposed to the threat of rapid catch-up by Chinese chipmakers like CXMT.
② Disproportionate Selling by Foreign Passive Funds
Whenever global funds scale back their risk asset portfolios, South Korean stocks bear the brunt first. Because rebalancing is straightforward and trading liquidity is abundant, aggressive selling is executed heavily across both spot and futures markets. In the first half of this month alone, net selling by foreign investors exceeded 18 trillion won. In contrast, the buying capacity of domestic institutional and retail investors to absorb this volume has been exhausted. As a result, price support lines collapsed helplessly.
③ Surging Exchange Rates and a Vicious Cycle of Margin Calls
The rising won-dollar exchange rate further incentivized foreign investors to sell to avert currency losses. On top of that, forced margin call liquidations from leveraged retail accounts flooded the market amid the steep drop. A technical downward spiral ensued, where declines triggered further declines.
① Concerns Over Entrenching Multi-Tiered Duplicate Listings
One of the unique structural afflictions of the South Korean market is the pyramidal governance structure connecting the holding company (SK Inc.), the intermediate holding company (SK Square), and the operating company (SK Hynix). Critics point out that separately listing Solidigm, a core subsidiary, would effectively create a four- to five-tier duplicate listing structure. Analysts warn that this could pile an extreme "holding company discount" onto the equity values of the parent company and upper-tier holding firms.
② Carve-Out of Core Growth Drivers and Equity Dilution
Solidigm initially posted substantial operating losses. However, fueled by surging demand for high-capacity enterprise solid-state drives (eSSDs) for AI data centers, it has recently emerged as a lucrative core asset for SK Hynix. Investors cannot help but feel betrayed, arguing that parent company shareholders bore the financial burden throughout the loss-making phase, only to have the rewards carved out via an external listing just as the company entered a period of massive profit recovery.
③ Conflicts of Interest Between Parent and Subsidiary
If listed on the U.S. Nasdaq, Solidigm's board of directors would be legally bound under U.S. law to prioritize the interests of Solidigm shareholders. Structural conflicts of interest would inevitably arise when negotiating wafer supply pricing, patent royalties, and next-generation technology licensing with the parent company. Critics argue this will become a factor undermining the shareholder value of the parent, SK Hynix. In response, SK Hynix maintains that "Solidigm is an independent overseas corporation acquired and cultivated from Intel's NAND division in 2020, rather than a physical spin-off of a domestic business division." It emphasizes that "this is a rational business decision aimed at raising massive AI investment capital in local U.S. markets without burdening domestic shareholders through rights offerings or taking on additional debt." However, SK Hynix shareholders have reacted with indignation, voicing criticism that this is "a classic chaebol-style financial maneuver in which controlling shareholders with low equity stakes dilute the economic interests of minority shareholders to attract outside capital while maintaining control over the parent company."
Net selling by foreign investors reaching trillions to tens of trillions of won is not driven merely by concerns over an economic slowdown. To a large extent, foreign active funds that entered temporarily on policy momentum are withdrawing capital after concluding that South Korean conglomerates have not changed their ingrained tendency to neglect minority shareholders. In bull markets or liquidity-driven rallies, corporate governance flaws and duplicate listing risks were overshadowed by steep earnings growth. Confronted with a triple burden of a global economic slowdown, an AI bubble debate, and intensifying semiconductor competition, however, investors are fleeing first from a market that fails to protect shareholders in times of crisis while looking out solely for the interests of controlling shareholder families. The controversy surrounding Solidigm's listing and the steep plunge in domestic stocks, led by SK Hynix, stand as clear proof.

articles.title: Samsung, SK hynix sell-off excessive as memory outlook stays strong: analysts - The Korea Times
articles.summary: Samsung, SK hynix sell-off excessive as memory outlook stays strong: analysts  The Korea Times
articles.full_text:
KOSPI snaps 7-session losing streak as chip stocks rebound
The recent steep sell-off in Samsung Electronics and SK hynix shares has been excessive, driven by a lack of buying support in the Korean market and weaker investor confidence rather than deteriorating earnings, market watchers said Friday.
Shares of the two semiconductor giants have fallen sharply this month amid a broader rout in the benchmark KOSPI, despite rising earnings forecasts fueled by strong artificial intelligence (AI) demand and tightening memory supply.
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix shares plunged 23.9 percent and 31.5 percent, respectively, over seven consecutive trading sessions starting Oct. 6, while KOSPI shed 1,449.52 points, or 21 percent.
On Friday, the market recovered some ground, with Samsung rising 2.62 percent and SK hynix gaining 0.79 percent as KOSPI rebounded 2.05 percent, snapping a seven-session losing streak.
Analysts say the widening gap between share prices and fundamentals has pushed valuations for the two chipmakers to relatively low levels.
"The recent sharp declines in Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are an excessive correction driven more by a lack of buying support in the Korean stock market and weakened investor sentiment than by a deterioration in fundamentals," Kim Dong-won, head of research at KB Securities, said in a report.
Kim said investors had priced in excessive concerns about a recession and falling corporate earnings, despite no clear signs of a deterioration in the semiconductor industry’s fundamentals.
SK Securities echoed the assessment, saying that the memory market remains on strong footing.
"Despite the won's appreciation, earnings forecasts for next year are being revised upward on expectations that the memory supply shortage will deepen more than previously anticipated and that prices of high-bandwidth memory will rise next year," analyst Han Dong-hee said.
The brokerage also maintained its view that long-term supply agreements would improve the sustainability of earnings and strengthen chipmakers' cash generating capacity, paving the way for higher shareholder returns.
"Now is the right time to buy memory stocks," Han said.
The analyst pointed to improving earnings estimates and potential shareholder returns as possible catalysts for a recovery. SK hynix is scheduled to announce its third-quarter earnings on Oct. 28, followed by Samsung Electronics on Oct. 29.
Meanwhile, the benchmark KOSPI, which plunged 7.57 percent the previous day amid concerns over AI-related spending and U.S. inflation, opened 1.8 percent higher at 5,653.99 and closed at 5,668.05, up 113.83 points, or 2.05 percent, from the previous session.
Retail investors and institutional investors were net sellers of 484.6 billion won ($ 363.3 million) and 683.3 billion won worth of shares, respectively, while foreign investors net purchased 341 billion won worth of shares.
Investor sentiment was buoyed by remarks from Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh at the International Monetary Fund’s annual meetings in Bangkok, Friday.
"The advent of this new technology is probably the most consequential change in the U.S. and the global economy in my lifetime," he said, describing AI as "a positive shock."
The tech-heavy Kosdaq also rebounded sharply after a steep fall in the previous session, closing at 794.78, up 33.96 points, or 4.46 percent. The index extended its gains largely on institutional buying, triggering a buy-sidecar activation at around 12:55 p.m.
The won strengthened against the dollar, with the exchange rate falling 13.2 won from the previous session to 1,331.4 won per dollar.

Global AI and semiconductor stocks extended their slide as concerns over higher interest rates, the cost of artificial intelligence investment and a potential challenge from Chinese memory makers converged.
CNBC reported on the 15th that the combined market value of the world's 20 largest AI and semiconductor stocks fell by $1 trillion (about 1,340 trillion won) over the four trading sessions from the 12th to the 15th.
Nvidia, the sector's bellwether, fell 5.3%, shedding about $291 billion (about 391 trillion won) in market value. SK hynix followed with a $243.8 billion decline and Samsung Electronics with $237.3 billion. Samsung Electronics, SK hynix and Micron Technology together accounted for about 40% of the total decline.
Data compiled by U.S. financial news outlet Benzinga showed a similar trend. The combined market value of six memory and storage companies — Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, Micron, Kioxia, SanDisk and Western Digital — has fallen $1.09 trillion (about 1,463 trillion won) since the 2nd.
On the New York market that day, Nvidia fell 1.8%, Intel lost 2.8% and AMD declined 1.5%, while Dell Technologies tumbled 6.8%.
Strong results from TSMC failed to lift sentiment. The chipmaker projected fourth-quarter revenue of as much as $54.3 billion (about 72.9 trillion won), above market expectations. Its shares still fell 2.0% in Taipei, and its American depositary receipts listed in New York dropped 1.8%.
Markets are being unsettled by views that the AI-driven supercycle is nearing its end. Others counter that prices are unlikely to collapse as they have in past downturns.
Behind the unease is the prospect of further rate increases by the Federal Reserve, which has raised concerns that financing costs for building AI data centers could climb. Competitive pressure has also grown after China's ChangXin Memory Technologies recently unveiled a new structural technology that raises memory density.
As that fueled arguments that memory supply could outstrip demand by 2029, Tesla Chief Executive Elon Musk responded in a post on X, formerly Twitter, saying China would produce an enormous amount of RAM in 2028.
Some analysts expect the shock from China to hit Korean companies hardest. Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, told CNBC that if there is an impact, it will show up at SK hynix and Samsung Electronics, not Micron. Micron swung between gains and losses during the session before closing 1.9% higher.

articles.title: BOJ may need to tighten faster if inflation beats forecast, IMF says - KWSN
articles.summary: BOJ may need to tighten faster if inflation beats forecast, IMF says  KWSN
articles.full_text:
By Leika Kihara
BANGKOK, Oct 17 (Reuters) – The Bank of Japan is “doing the right thing” by normalising monetary policy and may need to raise interest rates faster if inflation rises more than expected, a senior International Monetary Fund official told Reuters.
Japan must also clarify how it plans to fund its big spending plans and lay out a medium-term fiscal framework to ease market concerns about fiscal risks, said Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF’s Asia and Pacific Department.
“I would say that they are doing the right thing at this point,” Srinivasan said on the BOJ’s efforts to lift its policy rate towards levels deemed neutral to the economy.
“If inflation rises faster than expected, you have to start tightening faster because you don’t want inflation expectations to get un-anchored. It’s data dependent,” he said in an interview on Friday.
The remarks came ahead of the BOJ’s key policy meeting later this month, when it could keep rates steady but drop hawkish hints that would reinforce dominant market expectations of a December hike.
Inflationary pressures from the Middle East conflict and brisk AI-demand were among key themes discussed by policymakers gathering for this week’s annual IMF meetings in Bangkok.
BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda, who attended the IMF meetings, said on Friday the central bank will focus on anchoring underlying inflation around its 2% target and won’t tolerate any overshoot, stressing anew its resolve to continue raising interest rates.
For Japan, a weak yen adds to factors pushing up inflation by boosting the cost of raw material imports.
Such mounting price pressures prodded the BOJ to raise rates to a 31-year high of 1.25% in September, following a hike in June. Many analysts expect another rate increase by year-end.
Japan also conducted a rare, coordinated intervention with the US on July 31 to prevent the currency’s slide to near 40-year lows from destabilising financial markets.
In staff analysis included in its report on Asia’s economy, the IMF said a big portion of yen moves since mid-2025 had little to do with fundamental factors such as yield differentials, and instead co-moved with speculative positions in yen futures.
“Japan has a deep foreign exchange market, so as a first line of defense, they have allowed the exchange rate to move,” Srinivasan said.
“Bottom line, I would say that the Japanese authorities are fully committed to a freely floating exchange rate. I’ve had many discussions with them. So I don’t doubt that at all,” he said when asked if the recent yen intervention was justified.
FISCAL FRAMEWORK NEEDED
Rising global bond yields have also drawn attention at this week’s IMF meetings as debt in advanced economies, including Japan, expanded after years of heavy spending.
Markets worry that Japan may add to its already huge debt pile with the administration’s big spending plans and a two-year cut to the consumption tax from April next year.
Srinivasan said Japan has in fact seen fiscal consolidation proceed more than any other G7 country since the pandemic due in part to rising tax revenues.
“Markets are concerned about the fiscal risks because of the uncertainty” on how Japan would pay for the fresh spending and tax-cut plans, he said. “Japan also would benefit from having a medium-term fiscal framework.”
(Reporting by Leika Kihara; Editing by Sam Holmes)
